cardio-chest-pressure.title: Chest pressure on exertion
cardio-chest-pressure.blurb: Middle-aged adult with three weeks of exertional chest pressure that stops with rest.
cardio-chest-pressure.curriculum_note: Cardiovascular complaints and case are ILG 3 and ILG 4 on the PCM I schedule. Original case; not a prediction of any exam station.

doorway: Ray Delgado, 58-year-old male.
Presents to the family medicine clinic with chest pressure.
Vital signs are on the chart in the room.
Perform a focused history and physical examination, and discuss your plan with the patient.
You have 14 minutes.

patient.name: Ray Delgado
patient.persona: A warehouse supervisor who has been putting this off. Understated, minimises his symptoms, uses 'indigestion' rather than 'pain'. His wife made the appointment. Quietly frightened but reluctant to say so.
patient.affect: Calm and a little dismissive; opens up if asked directly what worries him.
patient.opening: I've been getting this pressure in my chest when I push myself at work. It goes away when I stop. My wife made me come in.
empathy_replies: I appreciate that. I've been trying not to think about it.
Thanks, doc. It's been on my mind more than I let on.
closing_questions: Is this my heart? My father died of a heart attack.
Do I need to stop working? I can't really afford to.

differentials.name: Stable angina pectoris
differentials.not_most_likely_because: The 2021 AHA/ACC Chest Pain Guideline draws the acute/stable line on CHANGE, not on whether pain occurs at rest: 'stable' is reserved for symptoms that are chronic with consistent precipitants. His symptoms are three weeks old and the threshold has fallen from heavy exertion to one flight of stairs - one flight of stairs is the operational definition of CCS class III. That makes this new-onset angina of at least CCS III AND crescendo angina, two of the three accepted unstable-angina presentations, neither of which requires rest pain. Absence of rest pain is the commonest reasoning error on this case; it is not reassurance.

model_note.S:
cc: Chest pressure with exertion for 3 weeks

HPI: 58 yo m with a history of HTN, hyperlipidemia and prediabetes presents to clinic c/o substernal chest pressure that started 3 weeks ago. Episodes are brought on by exertion - carrying boxes, climbing one flight of stairs - last about 5 minutes and resolve with rest. Pressure is described as a heaviness, 6/10 at worst, radiating to the left arm and intermittently to the jaw. Progressive: initially only with heavy exertion, now with less. Associated with exertional dyspnea, diaphoresis and mild nausea. Denies pain at rest, syncope, palpitations, orthopnea, PND and lower extremity edema. Not positional, not pleuritic, not related to meals. Antacids gave no relief. No prior similar episodes. Concerned this is his heart; his father died of an MI at 61.

PMH: HTN, hyperlipidemia, prediabetes.
PSH: Appendectomy age 20. No hospitalizations since.
Meds: Lisinopril 20 mg 1 tab daily; atorvastatin 40 mg 1 tab nightly. Not on aspirin.
SH: Warehouse supervisor. Current smoker, 1 ppd x 35 years. 2-3 beers most evenings. Denies illicit drug use including cocaine. Sedentary, poor diet.
FH: Father died of MI at 61. Mother 82 with HTN and DM. Brother 62 with a coronary stent.
Allergies: NKDA.
ROS: Cardiovascular - admits exertional chest pressure, dyspnea, diaphoresis; denies palpitations, syncope, orthopnea, edema. Respiratory - denies cough, hemoptysis and wheezing. GI - admits mild nausea; denies heartburn, vomiting and abdominal pain.
model_note.O:
Vitals: T 98.4 F oral, P 88 bpm, BP 158/94 mmHg, R 16 rpm, Pulse Ox 97% on room air, Ht 5'9", Wt 205 lbs

General: Overweight middle-aged man, comfortable at rest, in no acute distress. Alert and oriented.
Heart: RRR, S1 and S2 present with an S4 gallop, no murmurs or rubs. PMI non-displaced. No JVD at 30 degrees. Radial, dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses 2+ and symmetric, no carotid bruits.
Lungs: CTA bilaterally anterior and posterior. No rales, rhonchi or wheezes.
Chest wall: Non-tender to palpation; palpation does not reproduce the pain.
Abd: Bowel sounds present in 4 quadrants. Soft, non-tender including the epigastrium.
Exts: No lower extremity edema. No calf tenderness. Capillary refill under 2 seconds.
Osteopathic: T1-T5 left paraspinal tissue texture change, tenderness and restricted motion; T3 sidebent right, rotated right.
P: 1. Obtain a 12-lead ECG promptly and serial high-sensitivity troponin through the emergency team; assess current symptoms and vital signs, and arrange transfer to the emergency department now by EMS. Discuss aspirin only after allergy and bleeding review; anti-ischemic medicines require clinician review of blood pressure, possible severe aortic stenosis and relevant contraindications. Explain the worsening exertional pattern and why routine exercise stress testing is inappropriate before acute coronary syndrome is excluded.

2. Transthoracic echocardiogram of the heart with Doppler during this evaluation to measure aortic valve area, peak velocity and mean gradient and to assess left ventricular hypertrophy; cardiology to read it alongside the ischemic workup. No heavy exertion and no stair climbing until the valve is assessed. Educate that exertional chest pain, exertional shortness of breath and fainting are the three symptoms that change the prognosis of a stiff aortic valve, and that any near-faint means returning immediately.

3. Only after acute coronary syndrome is excluded: omeprazole 20 mg 1 tab daily 30 minutes before breakfast for an 8 week trial. Structured tobacco cessation with nicotine replacement, no food within 3 hours of lying down, and head of the bed elevated. OMT is deferred today; rib raising and paraspinal inhibition at T1-T5 may be offered once ischemia is excluded, because improvement after manual treatment cannot exclude ischemia. Educate that relief with an antacid or with OMT does not rule out heart disease.

ideal_encounter_extras: Ask explicitly whether he is on aspirin. It changes the plan and it is the kind of detail a differential-with-a-plan lives on.
Quantify the tobacco history in pack-years rather than 'he smokes' - the rubric asks for specific documentation.
Ask about cocaine by name in a chest pain case; 'do you use drugs' is easy to answer no to.
Palpate the chest wall deliberately and say what you are testing for. The value of this maneuver is the NEGATIVE, and a negative you can document is worth as much as a positive.
Ask what he thinks is going on before reassuring him. His answer is the F.I.F.E. item, and it is also the reason he finally came in.

model_note.S:
cc: Fever, cough and pain on deep breathing

HPI: 52 yo m. Patient reports: The cough began 4 days ago. The discomfort is in my right lower chest. The pain stays there. It is a sharp pain when I cough or breathe deeply. The pain is 5/10. The fever began the next day and the cough is getting worse. My coworker had a respiratory illness last week. Acetaminophen lowers the fever for a few hours. Coughing and deep breathing worsen the pain. I took acetaminophen 500 mg twice yesterday. I have not had pneumonia before. I cough up yellow sputum. I am short of breath on stairs. I measured 101.5 at home. I had shaking chills last night. I feel wiped out. The right chest pain is worse with a deep breath.

Patient perspective: Could I give this to the people at home?

PMH: No chronic lung or heart disease; vaccines not reviewed recently.

PSH: Hernia repair at age 30.

Meds: Acetaminophen as above; no daily prescription medications.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

SH: Smokes 5 cigarettes daily for 20 years. Two alcoholic drinks weekly. No recreational drugs. Bus dispatcher; lives with spouse; no recent travel, immobilization or surgery.

FH: Mother has asthma; father hypertension; one healthy sister.

ROS: Respiratory - Reports cough. Reports dyspnea. Denies hemoptysis. General - Reports fever. Reports chills. Reports fatigue. Cardiovascular - Reports chest pain. Denies edema. Denies syncope.
model_note.O:
Vitals: T 101.3 F oral, P 102 bpm, BP 122/76 mmHg, R 22 rpm, Pulse Ox 95% on room air, Ht 5' 7", Wt 165 lbs

General: Tired appearing, alert and oriented, speaking full sentences.

Heart: Regular tachycardia without murmur.

Lungs: Focal inspiratory crackles and bronchial breath sounds at the right posterior base. Dullness over the right posterior base compared with the left. Tactile fremitus is increased at the right posterior base.

Osteopathic: T1 paraspinal tissue texture change with mild tenderness on the right.

Skin: No visible rash on the inspected arms.
P: 1. Obtain chest x-ray and assess oxygenation, respiratory rate and severity to decide disposition; consider guideline-directed antibiotics after confirming the working diagnosis and allergy/comorbidity review; explain hydration and warning signs; reassess within 48–72 hours, sooner for worsening dyspnea, confusion or inability to drink.

2. Assess thromboembolic risk and use a validated diagnostic pathway if suspicion remains; obtain appropriate imaging rather than dismissing PE because fever is present; arrange urgent evaluation for clinical deterioration. If pulmonary embolism remains a concern, arrange emergency-department assessment; explain that fever does not rule out a clot and that increasing breathlessness or fainting requires immediate help.

3. Review smoking and persistent symptoms; ensure follow-up imaging or specialist evaluation if symptoms or consolidation do not resolve; offer smoking-cessation support and explain that cancer is a differential, not an established diagnosis.

cc: Breathlessness when lying down and swollen ankles

HPI: 67 yo f. Patient reports: This started 5 days ago. The breathlessness is in my chest; both ankles are swollen. There is no spreading chest pain. It feels like I cannot get enough air when flat. I now need 3 pillows and can walk only half a block. It has worsened each day and wakes me at night. I have been eating salty takeout while my kitchen is repaired. Sitting upright improves my breathing. Lying flat and walking make it worse. I tried sleeping in a chair. I had a milder episode last year. I need 3 pillows to sleep. I wake up gasping at night. Meds: Lisinopril 10 mg daily and furosemide 20 mg daily; missed furosemide for 4 days because the refill ran out.

FH: Mother had hypertension; father died after myocardial infarction at 72; brother has hypertension.

Vitals: T 98.4 F oral, P 98 bpm, BP 154/88 mmHg, R 22 rpm, Pulse Ox 94% on room air, Ht 5' 7", Wt 165 lbs

General: Alert and upright; mildly breathless while speaking.

Heart: Regular rhythm with S1, S2 and an audible S3. Jugular venous pressure is elevated with the head of the bed at 45 degrees.

P: 1. Arrange same-day emergency assessment for new/worsening congestion; obtain ECG, chest x-ray, CBC, BMP, natriuretic peptide and echocardiographic assessment; monitor oxygenation and renal function while clinician-directed diuresis is considered; explain fluid accumulation, review the missed refill and establish follow-up after stabilization.
2. Obtain chest x-ray and assess infection signs; use antimicrobials only if pneumonia is supported; counsel on returning immediately for worsening breathing or confusion.
3. Check creatinine, electrolytes, urinalysis and urine output; assess medication and volume history; involve nephrology if significant renal dysfunction is found and explain monitoring needs.

cc: Episodes of racing and irregular heartbeat

HPI: 46 yo m. Patient reports: The first episode was 2 weeks ago; this continuous episode began 6 hours ago. The fluttering is in the center of my chest. There is no pain spreading elsewhere. It feels fast and irregular rather than like one hard beat. This episode makes ordinary walking uncomfortable. Earlier episodes lasted 10 minutes, but this one is continuous. I was sitting at work when it began. Rest has not stopped this episode. Energy drinks seem to bring episodes on. I stopped drinking coffee today but it is still happening. These episodes are new; I had no earlier history of palpitations. My heart feels fast and uneven. I feel a little short of breath when walking. I have less energy today.

Patient perspective: Does this mean I am having a heart attack?

PMH: Hypertension; no known thyroid or structural heart disease.

PSH: No surgeries or hospitalizations.

Meds: Amlodipine 5 mg daily; no supplements or decongestants.

Allergies: Penicillin causes hives.

SH: Never smoked tobacco. Two beers most evenings. No cocaine, amphetamines or other recreational drugs. Software analyst; lives with spouse; drinks 3 energy drinks on workdays.

FH: Mother has hypertension; father has atrial fibrillation; sister is healthy; no sudden death before age 50.

ROS: Cardiovascular - Reports palpitations. Denies chest pain. Denies syncope. Respiratory - Reports dyspnea. Denies cough. Denies hemoptysis. General - Denies fever. Reports fatigue. Denies weight loss.
model_note.O:
Vitals: T 98.2 F oral, P 126 bpm, BP 124/78 mmHg, R 18 rpm, Pulse Ox 98% on room air, Ht 5' 7", Wt 165 lbs

General: Alert. Speaking comfortably at rest.

Heart: Tachycardic and irregularly irregular rhythm; no murmur heard.

Ext: Radial pulse is rapid and irregular.

Lungs: Bilateral breath sounds without crackles or wheeze.

HEENT: Thyroid not enlarged and nontender.

Osteopathic: T1 paraspinal tissue texture change with mild tenderness on the right.

Skin: No visible rash on the inspected arms.
P: 1. Obtain a 12-lead ECG now and assess hemodynamic stability; check BMP, magnesium, CBC and thyroid tests; arrange same-day emergency department evaluation for rate/rhythm and stroke-risk assessment; explain uncertainty until ECG confirmation and seek emergency help for chest pain, syncope or worsening dyspnea.

2. Review energy drinks, alcohol and sympathomimetic exposure; advise stopping energy drinks and discuss reducing alcohol; arrange symptom/rhythm follow-up rather than assuming all episodes are benign.
3. Obtain TSH with reflex thyroid hormones; examine for thyroid signs and review weight/heat intolerance; refer for targeted treatment if results support thyroid disease.

cc: Sudden breathlessness and pain with breathing

The pain is 6/10. The breathlessness has stayed constant since it began. I returned from an 8-hour flight 3 days ago. Sitting still helps a little. Deep breaths and walking make it worse. P: 1. Arrange immediate emergency evaluation; obtain ECG, chest x-ray and a validated pretest assessment to guide CTPA or D-dimer testing; discuss anticoagulation only after bleeding risk and urgent clinician evaluation; explain why a lung clot must be excluded and use EMS rather than self-driving.
2. Obtain chest x-ray and CBC during urgent assessment; consider antibiotics only if infection is supported; explain that fever may be absent and reassess the clinical course.
3. Urgently assess bilateral ventilation and obtain chest imaging if stable; involve the emergency team for decompression if tension physiology develops; explain return/emergency precautions.

cc: Lightheadedness after standing

HPI: 58 yo f. Patient reports: It began 3 days ago. It feels like lightheadedness in my head, not spinning. There is no pain radiating anywhere. My vision dims and I feel faint. It lasts about 20 seconds and I need to hold a chair. It happens after standing, then settles. My blood pressure medicine dose increased last week. Sitting or lying down makes it stop. Standing quickly and hot showers provoke it. I started standing more slowly. I have not had this before. My vision dims when I stand.

Patient perspective: I am scared I will fall while I am alone.

PMH: Hypertension; no heart disease or diabetes.

PSH: No operations or prior hospital admissions.

Meds: Hydrochlorothiazide increased from 12.5 mg to 25 mg daily last week.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

SH: Never smoked tobacco. One glass of wine weekly. No recreational drugs. Librarian; lives with partner; has been drinking less water to avoid bathroom trips.

FH: Mother has hypertension; father died of pneumonia at 80; one healthy brother.

ROS: Neurologic - Reports presyncope. Denies vertigo. Denies focal weakness. Cardiovascular - Denies syncope. Denies palpitations. Denies chest pain. Gastrointestinal - Denies melena. Denies vomiting. Denies diarrhea.
model_note.O:
Vitals: T 98.3 F oral, P 78 bpm, BP 126/76 mmHg seated, R 16 rpm, Pulse Ox 99% on room air, Ht 5' 7", Wt 165 lbs

General: Alert. Comfortable while seated.

Heart: Regular rhythm, S1 and S2 without murmur. After 5 minutes supine BP 126/76, pulse 78; at 1 minute standing BP 102/64, pulse 92 with lightheadedness; at 3 minutes standing BP 104/66, pulse 90.

Lungs: Breath sounds clear bilaterally.

Neuro: Strength 5/5 in both arms and legs.

Osteopathic: T1 paraspinal tissue texture change with mild tenderness on the right.

Skin: No visible rash on the inspected arms.
P: 1. Measure orthostatic vitals safely and obtain ECG, BMP and CBC; review the recent dose change with the prescribing clinician before altering therapy; discuss hydration if not contraindicated, slow standing and fall precautions; follow up within 48 hours and seek emergency care for syncope, chest pain or focal deficits.

2. Obtain ECG and consider ambulatory monitoring if unexplained or recurrent; assess exertional episodes and family sudden death; arrange cardiology review if rhythm or risk findings warrant it. Educate the patient to sit or lie down promptly if symptoms recur and to avoid situations in which another episode could cause injury while the cause is being assessed.

3. Check CBC and ask about blood loss; investigate any identified anemia rather than empirically treating without a cause; explain emergency precautions for bleeding or worsening weakness. Arrange follow-up to review the CBC and any bleeding history within 48 hours if stable enough for outpatient care; active bleeding or worsening presyncope requires immediate reassessment.

Assess hydration and ability to tolerate oral rehydration; consider BMP when dehydration is significant and targeted stool testing for severe, persistent or bloody illness rather than routinely; educate about oral rehydration, hand hygiene and warning signs; recheck within 24–48 hours and use urgent care for inability to drink, scant urine, bloody stool or worsening focal pain.

gi-epigastric-melena.blurb: Adult with weeks of burning epigastric pain and one black tarry stool.

doorway: Dana Whitfield, 41-year-old female.
Presents to the family medicine clinic with stomach pain.
Vital signs are on the chart in the room.
A point-of-care hemoglobin was drawn at check-in; the result is on the chart.

model_note.S:
cc: Burning epigastric pain for 6 weeks

HPI: 41 yo f with a history of osteoarthritis and migraines presents to clinic c/o burning epigastric pain that started 6 weeks ago and has been markedly worse over the past 3 days. Pain is midline epigastric, does not radiate, described as burning and gnawing, 7/10 at worst and 3/10 between episodes. Worse on an empty stomach and wakes her around 2 a.m.; relieved temporarily by food and by OTC antacids. Worse with coffee and on days she takes more ibuprofen. Reports one black tarry stool 2 days ago, which she attributed to iron tablets a friend gave her 1 week ago. Denies hematemesis and coffee-ground emesis. Associated with nausea, fatigue for 2-3 weeks, and lightheadedness on standing. Denies weight loss, dysphagia, jaundice, fever and diarrhea. No prior ulcer. Concerned this is stomach cancer; her mother died of gastric cancer at 68.

PMH: Osteoarthritis of both knees. Migraines.
PSH: Cholecystectomy age 35. Two vaginal deliveries.
Meds: Ibuprofen 800 mg 2-3 times daily for months; ferrous sulfate started 1 week ago. Not on a PPI.
SH: School administrator, lives with husband and two children. Never smoker. 1-2 glasses of wine on weekends. No illicit drug use.
FH: Mother died of gastric cancer at 68. Father 72 with HTN. One sister, healthy.
Allergies: Penicillin - lip and facial swelling.
ROS: GI - admits epigastric pain, nausea, melena; denies vomiting, hematemesis, dysphagia, diarrhea. General - admits fatigue; denies fever, weight loss, night sweats. Hematologic - admits lightheadedness and pallor; denies easy bruising, bleeding gums and nosebleeds.
model_note.O:
Vitals: T 98.2 F oral, P 96 bpm, BP 112/68 mmHg, R 16 rpm, Pulse Ox 98% on room air, Ht 5'4", Wt 152 lbs

General: Adult woman appearing tired and pale, alert and oriented, in no acute distress.
HEENT: Conjunctival pallor bilaterally. Sclerae anicteric. PERLA.
Heart: Mildly tachycardic, regular rhythm, S1 and S2 present, no murmurs, rubs or gallops.
Lungs: CTA bilaterally anterior and posterior. Good air movement.
Abd: Flat, no distention, well-healed laparoscopic scars RUQ and umbilicus. Hyperactive bowel sounds in 4 quadrants, no bruits. Tympanitic throughout, liver span approximately 9 cm. Soft with focal epigastric tenderness. No rebound, no guarding, no masses, no hepatosplenomegaly. Murphy sign negative. McBurney point non-tender.
Rectal: Refused at this time.
Skin: Pale. No telangiectasias, petechiae or bruising.
Labs: Point-of-care hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL.
Osteopathic: T5-T9 bilateral paraspinal tissue texture change and tenderness, left greater than right; T7 rotated left.
A: 1. NSAID-induced peptic ulcer disease with upper gastrointestinal bleeding
P: 1. Obtain CBC, BUN/creatinine, coagulation studies and type and screen; arrange emergency department evaluation today, vascular access and resuscitation as indicated, with gastroenterology consultation and endoscopy after stabilization. The known hemoglobin and melena already make a very-low-risk outpatient pathway inappropriate; calculate the complete bleeding risk assessment when missing values are available. A restrictive transfusion threshold around 7 g/dL is commonly used in stable hospitalized upper-GI bleeding, but ongoing hemorrhage, instability and cardiovascular disease change decisions. Stop ibuprofen; discuss clinician-directed acid suppression and non-NSAID analgesia. Educate about black tarry stools, hematemesis, syncope and the immediate disposition.

2. Biopsy at the time of that same endoscopy, including the ulcer margin and the gastric antrum and body; gastroenterology consultation in hospital. Treat H. pylori if the biopsy or stool antigen is positive, avoiding amoxicillin for her penicillin allergy, which caused lip and facial swelling. Educate on what the endoscopy involves and why her mother's gastric cancer at 68 makes a tissue diagnosis important. Repeat endoscopy in 8 to 12 weeks to document that the ulcer has healed.

3. Ferritin, iron, total iron binding capacity and reticulocyte count; serial hemoglobin during the admission. Resume oral iron with vitamin C after the endoscopy and educate on taking it with food to limit nausea. OMT is deferred while she is bleeding; rib raising and paraspinal inhibition to T5-T9 may be offered once she is stable. Educate that the fatigue and the lightheadedness on standing are from blood loss and should improve as the ulcer heals.

ideal_encounter_extras: Ask about stool colour explicitly. She will not volunteer the black stool - she has already explained it to herself as the iron tablets - and it is the single most important fact in the case.
Ask the dose and frequency of the ibuprofen, not just whether she takes 'anything for pain'. 800 mg three times daily for months is the diagnosis.
Ask the allergy reaction, not just the allergen. 'Penicillin - swelling' rules out standard triple therapy; 'penicillin - upset stomach' would not.
Inspect the conjunctivae. It is thirty seconds and it converts 'she says she is tired' into a documented physical finding.
Auscultate before you percuss or palpate. The hyperactive bowel sounds are a real finding here, and palpating first changes them.

model_note.S:
cc: Food sticking and unintentional weight loss

HPI: 63 yo m. Patient reports: It began 8 weeks ago. Food seems to stop behind my breastbone. There is no pain spreading to the arms or back. It feels like food sticks after I swallow. I have lost 10 pounds without trying. Solid food was the problem first; now soft foods are becoming difficult. I have had years of heartburn. Small bites and water sometimes help food pass. Meat and bread are hardest to swallow. Over-the-counter antacid helps heartburn but not the sticking. This progressive sticking is new. Solid food sticks after swallowing. Sometimes food comes back up. I lost 10 pounds in 2 months. I have less energy.

Patient perspective: My father had cancer. Is that what this is?

PMH: Longstanding reflux; no prior endoscopy.

PSH: No surgeries or admissions.

Meds: Calcium carbonate antacid as needed.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

SH: Smoked one pack daily for 30 years, quit 5 years ago. Two alcoholic drinks nightly. No recreational drugs. Retired mechanic; lives with spouse; still able to swallow liquids and manage saliva.

FH: Mother had stroke at 78; father died of lung cancer at 70; one healthy sister.

ROS: Gastrointestinal - Reports dysphagia. Denies odynophagia. Reports regurgitation. General - Reports weight loss. Reports fatigue. Denies fever. Respiratory - Denies cough. Denies dyspnea. Denies hemoptysis.
model_note.O:
Vitals: T 98.1 F oral, P 82 bpm, BP 124/76 mmHg, R 16 rpm, Pulse Ox 98% on room air, Ht 5' 7", Wt 165 lbs

General: Alert. Thin appearing; handles secretions without distress.

Heart: Regular rhythm without murmur.

Lungs: Clear breath sounds bilaterally.

HEENT: Oropharynx without visible lesions. No palpable cervical or supraclavicular nodes.

Abd: Abdomen not distended. Bowel sounds present. No focal tenderness with gentle palpation. Tympanic in examined quadrants.

Osteopathic: T5 paraspinal tissue texture change with mild tenderness on the right.

Skin: No visible rash on the inspected arms.
P: 1. Arrange expedited gastroenterology evaluation and upper endoscopy with biopsy as indicated; obtain CBC and nutritional assessment; explain that progressive dysphagia with weight loss requires prompt investigation but does not yet prove cancer; establish a specific referral follow-up and emergency advice for inability to swallow liquids or saliva.

2. Review reflux history and arrange endoscopic assessment to distinguish stricture from malignancy; consider clinician-directed acid suppression without delaying investigation; discuss safe textures pending specialist advice.
3. Clarify solids-versus-liquids chronology; pursue manometry after structural causes are evaluated if motility disorder remains likely; explain diagnostic uncertainty and specialist follow-up.

cc: Pain migrating to the right lower abdomen

model_note.O:
Vitals: T 100.6 F oral, P 106 bpm, BP 116/72 mmHg, R 18 rpm, Pulse Ox 99% on room air, Ht 5' 7", Wt 165 lbs

General: Alert. Uncomfortable, remaining still on the examination table.

Heart: Regular tachycardia without murmur.

Lungs: Breath sounds clear bilaterally.

Abd: Abdomen not distended; no surgical scars. Bowel sounds present. Focal right lower quadrant tenderness. Involuntary guarding in the right lower quadrant. Tenderness at McBurney point. Tympany over the examined quadrants.

Osteopathic: T5 paraspinal tissue texture change with mild tenderness on the right.

Skin: No visible rash on the inspected arms.
P: 1. Transfer to the emergency department immediately for surgical evaluation; obtain pregnancy testing, CBC, BMP, urinalysis and pregnancy-appropriate abdominal imaging; provide clinician-directed analgesia and fluids; explain concern for an acute abdominal process and use emergency disposition now.

2. Urgently obtain pregnancy test and pelvic ultrasound when indicated; involve obstetrics/gynecology for suspected ectopic pregnancy and monitor circulation; explain that pregnancy-related emergencies must be excluded despite uncertain pregnancy status.

3. Obtain urinalysis and pregnancy-appropriate renal imaging if the pattern suggests a stone; assess obstruction and infection, provide appropriate analgesia, and obtain urgent urology input for infected obstruction.

cc: Persistent right upper abdominal pain after eating

HPI: 44 yo f. Patient reports: It began 10 hours ago. It is under the right ribs. It travels toward my right shoulder blade. It is a steady deep ache. It is 8/10. It has stayed constant for hours. It began after a fatty meal. No position has relieved it. Taking a deep breath and eating worsen it. I tried an antacid without relief. I had two shorter episodes after meals last month. I feel nauseated. I vomited twice. I felt feverish this morning.

Patient perspective: Will I have to have surgery?

PMH: No known gallstones or chronic disease.

PSH: Cesarean delivery 12 years ago.

Meds: No daily medicines; one dose of antacid last night.

Allergies: Codeine causes severe nausea, without rash or breathing problems.

SH: Never smoked tobacco. One glass of wine monthly. No recreational drugs. Office manager; lives with spouse and child; last period 2 weeks ago, no pregnancy suspected.

FH: Mother had gallbladder surgery; father has diabetes; brother healthy.

ROS: Gastrointestinal - Reports nausea. Reports vomiting. Denies jaundice. General - Reports fever. Denies chills. Denies weight loss. Urinary - Denies dysuria. Denies hematuria. Denies frequency.
model_note.O:
Vitals: T 100.8 F oral, P 100 bpm, BP 128/78 mmHg, R 18 rpm, Pulse Ox 98% on room air, Ht 5' 7", Wt 165 lbs

General: Alert and uncomfortable, holding right upper abdomen.

Heart: Regular rhythm without murmur.

Lungs: Clear breath sounds at both posterior bases.

Abd: Abdomen not distended; healed lower abdominal scar. Bowel sounds present in all four quadrants. Right upper quadrant tenderness. Inspiratory arrest with right subcostal palpation during Murphy maneuver. Tympanitic away from the liver region.

HEENT: Conjunctivae pink and sclerae not icteric.

Osteopathic: T5 paraspinal tissue texture change with mild tenderness on the right.

Skin: No visible rash on the inspected arms.
P: 1. Transfer to the emergency department today for surgical evaluation of persistent pain and fever; obtain right upper quadrant ultrasound, CBC, liver tests, bilirubin and lipase; provide clinician-directed fluids and analgesia and consider antibiotics; explain why persistent pain differs from a brief uncomplicated biliary episode.

2. Obtain ECG and appropriate cardiac biomarkers if ischemia remains plausible; reassess cardiopulmonary symptoms and risk factors; explain that upper abdominal discomfort can occasionally come from the heart; consult the emergency/cardiology team for concerning findings.
3. Review NSAIDs and other irritants; consider acid suppression only after urgent causes are assessed; explain avoidance of unnecessary NSAIDs and follow-up for persistent symptoms.

model_note.S:
cc: Sudden arm weakness and difficulty speaking

HPI: 62 yo m. Patient reports: I was last completely well 45 minutes ago. My right arm and the right side of my face feel weak. There is no pain spreading anywhere. The arm feels heavy and difficult to lift. I dropped a mug and cannot write normally. It began suddenly and has not improved. It happened while eating breakfast; my spouse saw the onset. Rest has not helped. There is no movement trigger. I have taken no treatment for it. I had no previous episode like this. My right arm suddenly became weak. I have trouble finding the right words.

Patient perspective: Will I be able to speak normally again?

PMH: Hypertension and type 2 diabetes; no previous stroke.

PSH: No recent surgery or bleeding.

Meds: Metformin 500 mg twice daily and lisinopril 10 mg daily; no anticoagulant.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

SH: Smokes 10 cigarettes daily for 30 years. Two alcoholic drinks weekly. No cocaine or other recreational drugs. Retired delivery driver; lives with spouse who witnessed the onset.

FH: Mother had stroke at 70; father diabetes; brother hypertension.

ROS: Neurologic - Reports focal weakness. Reports speech change. Denies headache. Denies seizure. Cardiovascular - Denies palpitations. Denies chest pain. Denies syncope. General - Denies fever. Denies chills. Denies fatigue.
model_note.O:
Vitals: T 98.5 F oral, P 86 bpm, BP 168/94 mmHg, R 18 rpm, Pulse Ox 98% on room air, Ht 5' 7", Wt 165 lbs

General: Alert but has difficulty finding words.

Heart: Regular rhythm without murmur.

Lungs: Clear breath sounds bilaterally.

Neuro: Right lower facial weakness with forehead movement preserved; speech effortful. Right arm strength 3/5, left arm 5/5; both legs 5/5. Reduced light touch in the right hand compared with the left. Alert, recognizes self and location; naming is impaired.

Osteopathic: C1 paraspinal tissue texture change with mild tenderness on the right.

Skin: No visible rash on the inspected arms.
P: 1. Activate EMS/stroke pathway immediately; establish exact last-known-well and witness contact, obtain point-of-care glucose and urgent brain/vascular imaging through the stroke team; keep oral intake withheld until swallow safety is assessed; explain time-sensitive treatment eligibility and do not delay transfer to complete an elective exam or note.

2. Check bedside glucose immediately and treat a confirmed low value through the emergency team; reassess neurologic deficits afterward without abandoning stroke evaluation if they persist; explain that metabolic mimics need rapid testing.

3. Obtain urgent brain imaging through the stroke pathway to assess structural causes; involve neurology if a mass is identified; explain that this lower-probability possibility cannot be confirmed by the history and must not delay emergency assessment.

cc: Back pain with new bladder difficulty and leg symptoms

HPI: 43 yo m. Patient reports: The back pain began 3 days ago; the urinary difficulty began 6 hours ago. The pain is in the lower back. It runs down the backs of both legs. It is a severe deep pain with shooting leg pain. It is 8/10. The leg symptoms and bladder trouble are new today. It began after lifting a heavy box. Lying still helps only a little. Bending and coughing worsen the shooting pain. I took ibuprofen 400 mg twice without much relief. Previous back strains resolved without urinary difficulty; this episode is different. My low back hurts and shoots into both legs. The area between my legs feels numb when I wipe. Both feet feel weaker than usual. I have a full bladder feeling but can pass only drops.

Patient perspective: Can I just get my back adjusted?

PMH: Previous mechanical back pain; no cancer, diabetes or immune suppression.

PSH: No spine surgery or recent procedures.

Meds: Ibuprofen 400 mg twice today; no anticoagulants.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

SH: Never smoked tobacco. Two alcoholic drinks weekly. No injection or other recreational drug use. Warehouse supervisor; lives with spouse.

FH: Mother hypertension; father healthy; brother healthy; no known hereditary neurologic illness.

ROS: Neurologic - Reports back pain. Reports saddle numbness. Reports leg weakness. Urinary - Reports retention. Denies dysuria. Denies hematuria. General - Denies fever. Denies chills. Denies weight loss.
model_note.O:
Vitals: T 98.6 F oral, P 92 bpm, BP 138/84 mmHg, R 18 rpm, Pulse Ox 99% on room air, Ht 5' 7", Wt 165 lbs

General: Alert and uncomfortable, moving cautiously.

Heart: Regular rhythm without murmur.

Lungs: Clear breath sounds bilaterally.

MSK: Lower lumbar paraspinal tenderness.

Neuro: Bilateral ankle dorsiflexion 4/5; proximal leg strength 5/5. Reduced light touch along the lateral feet bilaterally. Achilles reflexes reduced bilaterally; patellar reflexes preserved.

Abd: Suprapubic fullness and discomfort on gentle palpation.

Osteopathic: C1 paraspinal tissue texture change with mild tenderness on the right.

Skin: No visible rash on the inspected arms.
A: 1. Cauda equina compression from lumbar disc herniation
P: 1. Transfer to the emergency department immediately for spine assessment and urgent lumbar MRI; document exact onset of bladder and saddle symptoms and assess motor/sensory deficits without delaying transfer; explain possible nerve compression and need for urgent specialist decisions; avoid spinal manipulation or a routine wait-and-see plan.

2. Review fever, injection drug use, immune suppression and procedures; obtain urgent lumbar MRI and infection testing through the emergency team if indicated; explain that lack of fever alone cannot exclude serious spinal infection.

3. Ask cancer and constitutional history and obtain urgent imaging for neurologic compression; involve the relevant spine/oncology teams if supported; explain that malignancy is a possibility to assess, not a known result.

cc: Gradual tingling and numbness in both feet

HPI: 57 yo f. Patient reports: It started 4 months ago. It began in the toes of both feet. It has spread up to the ankles, not into my hands. It is tingling, burning and reduced feeling. Burning is 5/10 at night. It has gradually spread and is now present daily. There was no injury. Taking the bedsheet off my feet helps. The bedsheet touching my feet and nighttime worsen it. I tried a foot cream without benefit. I have not had this before. Both feet feel numb. They tingle and burn at night. I have been more thirsty lately.

model_note.O:
Vitals: T 98.2 F oral, P 78 bpm, BP 136/82 mmHg, R 16 rpm, Pulse Ox 98% on room air, Ht 5' 7", Wt 165 lbs

General: Alert and comfortable at rest.

Heart: Regular rhythm without murmur.

Lungs: Clear breath sounds bilaterally.

Neuro: Reduced light touch and vibration symmetrically from toes to ankles. Achilles reflexes reduced bilaterally; patellar reflexes 2+. Lower extremity strength 5/5 bilaterally.

Skin: Skin of feet intact, without visible ulceration.

Ext: Dorsalis pedis pulses palpable and symmetric.

Osteopathic: C1 paraspinal tissue texture change with mild tenderness on the right.
P: 1. Assess symmetric sensory loss, foot integrity and gait; obtain A1c and review diabetes management and renal function; discuss individualized neuropathic-pain treatment with clinician review, daily foot checks and protective footwear; follow up in 2–4 weeks and seek prompt care for wounds, rapidly progressive weakness or falls.
2. Check B12 and CBC, particularly with long-term metformin use; replace a confirmed deficiency and investigate its cause; explain that more than one contributor may coexist.

3. Review neurotoxic drugs, supplements and alcohol exposure; do not stop necessary medication without prescriber review; arrange further neurologic testing if the pattern is atypical or progresses. Refer to neurology for atypical or progressive deficits and consider nerve conduction studies when needed to clarify the pattern; educate the patient to review supplements and drug exposures with the prescribing clinician rather than stopping necessary treatment independently.

cc: Brief spinning episodes when turning in bed

HPI: 56 yo f. Patient reports: It began 3 days ago. It feels like the room spins around me. There is no radiating pain. It is spinning rather than feeling faint. Each episode lasts about 20 seconds. It only happens with certain head movements; I feel well between spells. It first happened rolling onto my right side in bed. Keeping my head still stops it. Rolling right or looking up brings it on. I have avoided those movements. I have never had this before. Turning my head causes brief spinning. I feel briefly nauseated during a spell.

Patient perspective: I think I might be having a stroke.

PMH: No stroke, migraine or cervical spine disease.

PSH: No surgeries or admissions.

Meds: No daily medicines or sedatives.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

SH: Never smoked tobacco. One alcoholic drink weekly. No recreational drugs. School administrator; lives with spouse.

FH: Mother has hypertension; father had diabetes; one healthy sister.

ROS: Neurologic - Reports vertigo. Denies focal weakness. Denies diplopia. Gastrointestinal - Reports nausea. Denies vomiting. Denies abdominal pain. Cardiovascular - Denies syncope. Denies palpitations. Denies chest pain.

Vitals: T 98.2 F oral, P 76 bpm, BP 126/78 mmHg, R 16 rpm, Pulse Ox 99% on room air, Ht 5' 7", Wt 165 lbs

General: Alert and comfortable with head still.

Right Dix–Hallpike after suitability review elicits brief vertigo and transient upbeating torsional nystagmus after a short latency. Left Dix–Hallpike after suitability review does not elicit vertigo or nystagmus.

Osteopathic: C1 paraspinal tissue texture change with mild tenderness on the right.

Skin: No visible rash on the inspected arms.
P: 1. Assess neurologic red flags and cervical suitability, then perform a trained positional assessment; discuss canalith repositioning by a trained clinician if findings support posterior-canal BPPV; educate on temporary fall/driving precautions while symptomatic and arrange reassessment within 1 month; seek urgent care for persistent vertigo with new focal deficits or inability to walk.

2. Escalate immediately for acute focal deficits, severe gait impairment or a concerning persistent syndrome; obtain stroke-team evaluation and appropriate imaging; educate the patient about urgent neurologic warning signs; do not use a normal basic examination or an untrained HINTS assessment to exclude stroke.

3. Clarify whether vertigo is continuous for days rather than brief triggered spells; assess hearing and neurologic findings and arrange clinician evaluation; explain why the current time course is less typical for neuritis. Arrange reassessment if symptoms become persistent, hearing changes develop, or function worsens; persistent symptoms warrant a focused hearing and vestibular evaluation after urgent central causes have been considered.

Acetaminophen 500 mg helped a little. I have had the same pattern since age 19. It is the same left-sided throbbing pattern as before. Light hurts my eyes. I feel nauseated.

Patient perspective: Do I need a brain scan every time this happens?

PMH: Previously diagnosed migraine; no malignancy or immunosuppression.

PSH: No surgeries or hospitalizations.

Meds: Acetaminophen on 2–3 days per month; no daily medication.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

SH: Never smoked tobacco. One alcoholic drink monthly. No recreational drugs. Medical student; lives with roommate; regular periods, last period 2 weeks ago; pregnancy not suspected.

FH: Mother has migraine; father hypertension; brother healthy.

ROS: Neurologic - Reports headache. Reports photophobia. Denies focal weakness. Denies thunderclap. Gastrointestinal - Reports nausea. Denies vomiting. Denies abdominal pain. General - Denies fever. Denies chills. Denies weight loss.
model_note.O:
Vitals: T 98.4 F oral, P 78 bpm, BP 114/72 mmHg, R 16 rpm, Pulse Ox 99% on room air, Ht 5' 7", Wt 165 lbs

General: Alert. Prefers dim light, not toxic appearing.

Heart: Regular rhythm without murmur.

Lungs: Clear breath sounds bilaterally.

HEENT: Pupils equal and reactive; extraocular movements intact.

Neuro: Face symmetric; tongue midline; speech clear. Strength 5/5 in arms and legs bilaterally. Light touch symmetric in arms and legs. Neck flexion is comfortable without stiffness.

Osteopathic: C1 paraspinal tissue texture change with mild tenderness on the right.

Skin: No visible rash on the inspected arms.
P: 1. Review headache red flags, neurologic findings and pregnancy/medication contraindications; offer an individualized acute migraine treatment plan with clinician review and discuss nausea management; use a headache diary, regular meals and sleep, with follow-up in 2–4 weeks; explain emergency evaluation for a new sudden maximal headache, fever with stiff neck or focal deficit.

2. Assess fever, meningismus and systemic risk; urgent emergency evaluation and appropriate testing if infection is suspected; explain that the current absence of these features reduces but does not independently eliminate concern. If infection becomes a clinical concern, obtain blood cultures and consider lumbar puncture through the emergency team after safety assessment; testing must not delay urgent treatment.

3. Quantify every acute-medication day per month; counsel on avoiding escalation and arrange review if headache frequency or medication use increases; do not diagnose medication overuse from occasional use alone. Keep a headache and medication-day diary and arrange primary-care follow-up to review it in 4 weeks; refer to neurology if headaches become frequent or disabling despite initial management.

model_note.S:
cc: Sudden severe headache for 6 hours

HPI: 32 yo f with a 15-year history of migraines presents to clinic c/o a headache that began 6 hours ago while lifting a box and reached maximum intensity in under one minute. Pain is occipital, radiating into the neck, 10/10, constant and unrelenting since onset. She describes it as the worst headache of her life and explicitly unlike her usual migraine, which builds over hours, is unilateral and responds to sumatriptan. Sumatriptan taken 2 hours ago and ibuprofen 800 mg gave no relief. Worse with light, bending forward and coughing. Associated with neck stiffness, two episodes of vomiting without preceding nausea, and a transient greying of vision at onset without a fall. Denies focal weakness, numbness, speech change, visual change, seizure, fever, chills, rash, sick contacts and head trauma. Concerned this is a ruptured aneurysm; her mother had one at 49.

PMH: Migraines since age 17. No hypertension.
PSH: None. No hospitalizations.
Meds: Sumatriptan 100 mg PRN; ibuprofen 800 mg PRN; oral contraceptive 1 tab daily.
SH: Graphic designer, lives with her partner. Current smoker, 0.5 ppd x 10 years. Wine a few times weekly. Denies illicit drug use including cocaine and stimulants. LMP 2 weeks ago, no chance of pregnancy.
FH: Mother with a ruptured cerebral aneurysm at 49, survived. Father 61, well. One brother, healthy.
Allergies: NKDA.
ROS: Neurologic - admits headache, photophobia, transient near-syncope; denies weakness, numbness, seizure, speech change. HEENT - admits neck stiffness and photophobia; denies visual change and diplopia. General - admits vomiting; denies fever, chills, night sweats and weight loss.
model_note.O:
Vitals: T 98.8 F oral, P 92 bpm, BP 162/95 mmHg, R 16 rpm, Pulse Ox 99% on room air, Ht 5'6", Wt 141 lbs

General: Young woman lying still with eyes closed, shielding them from the light, in moderate distress from pain. Alert, oriented and answering appropriately.
HEENT: PERLA. Fundoscopy limited by photophobia; no papilledema seen in the portion visualised. Corneal reflex refused.
Neck: Marked resistance and pain on passive flexion. Rotation comfortable. Kernig and Brudzinski negative.
Heart: RRR, S1 and S2 present, no murmurs, rubs or gallops.
Lungs: CTA bilaterally anterior and posterior.
Neuro: CN II-XII intact as tested - visual fields full, EOM intact, facial sensation and strength symmetric, palate elevates symmetrically, tongue midline. Strength 5/5 in all four extremities, no pronator drift. Sensation to light touch and pinprick intact and symmetric. DTRs 2+ and symmetric at biceps, triceps, patellae and Achilles; plantars downgoing. Finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin intact, Romberg negative. Gait steady though guarded.
Skin: No rash, petechiae or purpura.
Osteopathic: Marked suboccipital and cervical paraspinal hypertonicity with tenderness, C1-C4; T1-T4 paraspinal tissue texture change. Cervical motion guarded.
P: 1. Transfer immediately to the emergency department by EMS for urgent noncontrast head CT and specialist assessment. Additional testing after a negative head CT depends on time from onset, imaging quality and residual suspicion; discuss lumbar puncture and/or vascular imaging through the emergency team rather than treating every negative CT identically. Obtain CBC, BMP and coagulation testing as appropriate; provide clinician-directed symptom control. Explain that a thunderclap headache cannot wait and the patient must not drive; emergency department disposition now.

2. Lumbar puncture with cell count, glucose, protein and culture as above; do not delay empiric antibiotics if fever or clinical deterioration develops; educate the patient and her partner on the warning signs of deterioration.

3. MRI of the brain with contrast once the emergency evaluation is complete; discontinue the combined oral contraceptive; refer to neurology; educate on smoking cessation, which compounds the same vascular risk.
OMT deferred: no cervical manipulation until an intracranial bleed is excluded.

ideal_encounter_extras: Ask how fast the headache reached its peak, not just when it started. 'Sudden' and 'maximal within a minute' are different claims, and only the second one is a thunderclap.

Ask how this headache differs from her usual migraine. A fifteen-year migraine history is the reason a clinician might dismiss this, and her own answer is the strongest argument against dismissing it.
Test neck flexion specifically. Rotation is comfortable here; only flexion demonstrates the finding.
Ask about the oral contraceptive and smoking together - they are the venous sinus thrombosis limb of the differential.
Propose the corneal reflex out loud so the refusal is on the record and can be documented.
This plan needs a disposition, not an interval. The rubric accepts 'admit to hospital' in place of 'follow up in 1 month', and this is the case that calls for it.

Note the tension this case creates: clinically, the three most dangerous possibilities here are all vascular, but the rubric requires three different VINDICATE elements. The model note resolves it with subarachnoid hemorrhage (Vascular), bacterial meningitis (Infectious) and an intracranial mass lesion (Neoplastic) - all defensible, all different. If your facilitator reads the requirement differently, the setting is configurable.

cc: Unable to urinate with lower abdominal pressure

HPI: 69 yo m. Patient reports: I last passed urine normally 10 hours ago. The pressure is low in the center of my abdomen. There is no flank radiation. It is a tight, painful fullness. The pressure is 8/10. It has become worse through the day. I started an over-the-counter cold medicine yesterday. Trying again does not relieve it. The fullness keeps increasing. I have tried to urinate several times without success. For months I have had a weak stream but never complete blockage. I cannot pass urine despite a strong urge. My stream has been slow to start for months.

Patient perspective: Will a catheter hurt?

PMH: Enlarged prostate diagnosed 2 years ago; no neurologic disease.

PSH: No pelvic surgery or catheterization history.

Meds: No prescribed prostate medicine; took diphenhydramine 25 mg last night for cold symptoms.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

SH: Quit tobacco 20 years ago after 10 pack-years. One alcoholic drink weekly. No recreational drugs. Retired engineer; lives with spouse.

FH: Father had prostate enlargement; mother had hypertension; brother healthy.

ROS: Urinary - Reports retention. Reports hesitancy. Denies hematuria. Neurologic - Denies back pain. Denies saddle numbness. Denies leg weakness. General - Denies fever. Denies chills. Denies fatigue.
model_note.O:
Vitals: T 98.6 F oral, P 94 bpm, BP 148/86 mmHg, R 18 rpm, Pulse Ox 98% on room air, Ht 5' 7", Wt 165 lbs

General: Alert and distressed by lower abdominal pressure.

Heart: Regular rhythm without murmur.

Lungs: Clear breath sounds bilaterally.

Abd: Visible lower midline abdominal fullness. Bowel sounds present. Tender rounded fullness in the suprapubic region. Dull percussion over the suprapubic fullness.

Neuro: Lower extremity strength 5/5 bilaterally.

Osteopathic: T10 paraspinal tissue texture change with mild tenderness on the right.

Skin: No visible rash on the inspected arms.
P: 1. Arrange immediate clinical bladder decompression assessment; obtain bladder volume measurement, renal function and urinalysis without delaying urgent treatment; review diphenhydramine and avoid further anticholinergic exposure pending clinician advice; explain retention and arrange urology follow-up after catheter planning and monitored recovery.

2. Review prostate and constitutional symptoms and arrange appropriate urology assessment after decompression; discuss prostate testing through shared decision-making; explain that obstruction does not itself establish cancer.

3. Review diabetes symptoms and neurologic history; obtain glucose and assess bladder emptying after acute treatment; arrange targeted evaluation if persistent dysfunction suggests a neurologic or metabolic cause. Refer to urology if bladder emptying remains impaired after acute treatment; educate the patient that diabetes-related nerve dysfunction is a possibility requiring evidence, not a diagnosis established by retention alone.

model_note.S:
cc: Severe flank pain that comes in waves

HPI: 41 yo m. Patient reports: It started suddenly 4 hours ago. It is in my left flank. It travels toward my left groin. It is sharp and cramping in waves. At its worst it is 9/10. Each wave lasts several minutes with partial easing between. It started while I was at work, without trauma. Nothing reliably relieves it. There is no clear movement trigger. I tried acetaminophen 500 mg without relief. I passed a kidney stone 5 years ago. The left flank hurts in waves. My urine looked pink once. I feel nauseated with the pain. I vomited once. The pain is exhausting.

Patient perspective: Will this damage my kidney?

PMH: One prior calcium kidney stone; has two kidneys; no kidney disease.

PSH: No surgery or admissions except the prior stone visit.

Meds: No daily medicines; acetaminophen once today.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

SH: Never smoked tobacco. Two alcoholic drinks weekly. No recreational drugs. Construction estimator; often cannot take water breaks; lives with partner.

FH: Father has recurrent kidney stones; mother has hypertension; sister healthy.

ROS: Urinary - Reports flank pain. Reports hematuria. Denies dysuria. Gastrointestinal - Reports nausea. Reports vomiting. Denies diarrhea. General - Denies fever. Denies chills. Reports fatigue.
Urinary history: I am still able to pass urine.
model_note.O:
Vitals: T 98.7 F oral, P 98 bpm, BP 142/86 mmHg, R 20 rpm, Pulse Ox 99% on room air, Ht 5' 7", Wt 165 lbs

General: Alert. Restless, frequently changing position.

Heart: Regular rhythm without murmur.

Lungs: Clear breath sounds bilaterally.

Abd: Abdomen not distended. Bowel sounds present. Mild left lateral abdominal tenderness. No involuntary guarding. Tympanic over examined quadrants. Left costovertebral angle tenderness; right side nontender.

Osteopathic: T10 paraspinal tissue texture change with mild tenderness on the right.

Skin: No visible rash on the inspected arms.
P: 1. Assess pain control, hydration, urine output, solitary kidney and infection risk; obtain urinalysis, creatinine and appropriate renal imaging; provide clinician-directed analgesia and antiemetic, with urgent urology for infected obstruction or renal compromise; explain urine straining if discharged and arrange prompt follow-up, with emergency return for fever or inability to urinate.

2. Obtain urine culture if infection is suspected and monitor systemic features; an obstructed infected urinary system needs urgent drainage evaluation rather than antibiotics alone; explain the fever/rigor emergency precaution.

3. Ask about mechanical triggers and assess focal musculature after urgent renal causes; consider conservative treatment only if supported; advise reassessment for new urinary or systemic features. If urgent renal causes are excluded and a muscular cause is supported, advise continued gentle daily activity as tolerated and avoidance of prolonged bed rest.

model_note.S:
cc: Burning urination without systemic symptoms

HPI: 29 yo f. Patient reports: The burning began 2 days ago. It burns at the urethra when I pass urine. There is no pain into my back or groin. It is a stinging burning sensation. The burning is 4/10 and I urinate about every hour. It happens with every urination. It started after intercourse but there was no injury. Drinking water makes the urine sting a little less. Urinating triggers it. I have increased fluids but taken no medicine. I had one bladder infection 3 years ago. It burns when I urinate. I need to go every hour. I get sudden urges to go. There is mild low abdominal pressure.

Patient perspective: Do I have a kidney infection?

PMH: No diabetes, kidney disease or immunosuppression.

PSH: No surgery or hospitalizations.

Meds: No daily medicines.

Allergies: Sulfonamide antibiotic caused hives.

SH: Never smoked tobacco. One alcoholic drink weekly. No recreational drugs. Graphic designer; lives alone; one established partner; uses condoms; last menstrual period 2 weeks ago, pregnancy not suspected.

FH: Mother has hypertension; father and brother are healthy.

ROS: Urinary - Reports dysuria. Reports frequency. Reports urgency. Denies flank pain. General - Denies fever. Denies chills. Denies fatigue. Gastrointestinal - Denies nausea. Denies vomiting. Reports abdominal pain.
model_note.O:
Vitals: T 98.4 F oral, P 78 bpm, BP 116/72 mmHg, R 16 rpm, Pulse Ox 99% on room air, Ht 5' 7", Wt 165 lbs

General: Alert. Comfortable and well hydrated.

Heart: Regular rhythm without murmur.

Lungs: Clear breath sounds bilaterally.

Abd: Abdomen not distended. Bowel sounds present. Mild suprapubic tenderness. Tympanic over the examined quadrants. No tenderness with gentle bilateral costovertebral angle percussion.

Osteopathic: T10 paraspinal tissue texture change with mild tenderness on the right.

Skin: No visible rash on the inspected arms.
P: 1. Obtain urinalysis and assess pregnancy possibility and complicated-infection features; choose an appropriate lower-UTI antibiotic after allergy and local-resistance review, avoiding sulfonamides; explain hydration, expected improvement and warning signs; reassess in 48–72 hours if not improving and seek prompt care for fever, flank pain or vomiting.

2. Assess colicky pain and hematuria and obtain urinalysis; use renal imaging only when the clinical picture warrants it; explain urgent precautions for severe pain, fever or inability to urinate; arrange urology evaluation if obstruction or persistent stone symptoms are found.

3. Ask about new soaps, spermicides and local irritants; discontinue a suspected irritant and assess genital symptoms as appropriate; educate on avoiding the identified irritant and arrange reassessment within 48–72 hours; refer for persistent symptoms rather than labeling a UTI without evidence.

model_note.S:
cc: Burning with urination for 2 days and right-sided back pain for 1 day

HPI: 24 yo f with no chronic medical conditions presents to clinic c/o burning with urination that started 2 days ago and right flank pain that started yesterday. Symptoms are progressively worsening. Flank pain is located in the right flank below the ribs, radiates toward the right groin, is a dull constant ache rated 7/10 (worst 8/10). Dysuria is burning, 5/10, only with voiding. Worse with movement and jarring; partially relieved by ibuprofen and a heating pad. Associated with subjective fever, shaking chills last night, nausea with one episode of emesis this morning, urinary frequency and urgency, and cloudy malodorous urine. Denies gross hematuria. Had a bladder infection 6 months ago treated with antibiotics; never involved the back. Tried ibuprofen, cranberry juice and increased fluids without relief. Concerned this is damaging her kidneys because an aunt required dialysis.

PMH: No chronic medical conditions. UTI 6 months ago.
PSH: Wisdom tooth extraction age 18. No hospitalizations.
Meds: Oral contraceptive 1 tab daily; ibuprofen 400 mg a couple of times daily for the past 2 days.
SH: Graduate student, lives with a roommate. Never smoker. 2-3 alcoholic drinks on weekends. No illicit drug use. Sexually active with one male partner, inconsistent condom use, no new partners. LMP 3 weeks ago, regular; pregnancy possible.
FH: Mother 52 with HTN. Father 55 with type 2 DM. One older brother, healthy. No kidney disease or stones in parents or brother; maternal aunt required dialysis, cause unknown.
Allergies: Sulfa - hives.
ROS: GU - admits dysuria, frequency, urgency; denies gross hematuria. GI - admits nausea and vomiting; denies diarrhea and constipation. General - admits subjective fever and chills; denies weight loss. Denies vaginal discharge, cough, chest pain, rash, headache.
model_note.O:
Vitals: T 101.6 F oral, P 104 bpm, BP 112/70 mmHg, R 18 rpm, Pulse Ox 99% on room air, Ht 5'5", Wt 138 lbs

General: Young woman appearing uncomfortable, shifting in the chair, in mild distress. Alert and oriented.
Heart: Tachycardic, regular rhythm, S1 and S2 present, no murmurs, rubs or gallops.
Lungs: CTA bilaterally anterior and posterior. Good air movement. No rales, rhonchi or wheezes.
Abd: Bowel sounds present and normoactive in 4 quadrants, no bruits. Tympanitic throughout. Soft, non-distended. Tenderness RUQ and right flank. No rebound, no guarding, no masses, no organomegaly. Murphy sign negative. McBurney point non-tender.
GU: Right CVA tenderness markedly positive; left CVA non-tender. Pelvic exam refused.
Skin: No rashes or lesions.
Labs: Point-of-care urine dipstick - leukocyte esterase positive, nitrites positive, trace blood, trace protein, glucose negative.
Osteopathic: T10-L1 right paraspinal tissue texture change, tenderness and hypertonicity; T11 rotated right.
P: 1. Obtain urine culture and urinalysis, pregnancy test, CBC and BMP; assess current stability, oral intake, obstruction and sepsis risk. Choose a renal-tissue-penetrating antibiotic through the clinician using allergy, pregnancy, local resistance and culture information; avoid the reported sulfonamide allergen. Do not use nitrofurantoin to treat pyelonephritis. Arrange emergency evaluation now if unstable, unable to retain fluids or at risk of infected obstruction; otherwise establish follow-up in 48–72 hours with culture review. Educate on the prescribed course, hydration and urgent deterioration precautions.

2. Assess for a ureteral stone with appropriate renal imaging when obstruction is suspected; provide clinician-directed analgesia and antiemetic and consult urology urgently for infected obstruction. Explain that fever with obstruction cannot be managed by hydration alone; defer manipulative treatment during acute systemic illness.

3. Obtain pregnancy testing and urgent pelvic ultrasound with Doppler if torsion remains clinically suspected; seek urgent gynecology evaluation based on suspicion rather than waiting for a reassuring Doppler result. Provide clinician-directed pain control and educate about sudden severe pelvic pain and emergency return.

P: 1. Obtain urinalysis with microscopy, renal function and CBC as appropriate; arrange prompt urology evaluation for cystoscopy and risk-appropriate upper-tract imaging; explain that painless visible blood still needs investigation and does not prove cancer; confirm referral tracking and emergency precautions for clots, inability to void, dizziness or heavy bleeding.

2. Use urine culture when infection is supported by symptoms or urinalysis; avoid assuming infection without evidence; ensure hematuria is reassessed even if an infection is treated. Educate the patient that an apparent infection does not eliminate the need to confirm resolution of visible blood; arrange follow-up after any treatment to review repeat urinalysis and pursue urology assessment if blood persists or recurs.
3. Review stone symptoms and select renal imaging when clinically indicated; assess obstruction and infection risk; explain prompt reassessment for pain, fever or reduced urine output.

reasoning_steps.question: Which encounter event supports this statement?
reasoning_steps.why: Separate reported symptoms, observed findings, interpretations and future actions. A true case fact is not documentation evidence until obtained.

rubric_connections.Subjective: Age/sex; complaint; chronology, quality, severity, modifiers; PMH/PSH, meds, allergies, social/family and three pertinent ROS systems.
rubric_connections.Objective: Vitals first; observed general, heart/lungs, focused and other examinations; level/descriptor only if actually examined.
rubric_connections.Assessment: Three numbered correlated differentials and distinct VINDICATE categories; uncertain mnemonic placements are explicitly provisional.
rubric_connections.Plan: Three numbered paired plans with at least three MOTHERR elements each; specific education and follow-up/disposition in Plan1.

teaching.classification_note: VINDICATE is an organizing mnemonic, not proof of etiology; these original cases are not faculty-approved answer keys.
recovery_routine: Pause and take one slow breath.
Name the phase you are in.

reasoning_map.question: Is the blood definitely in urine, does it recur, and are there clots or difficulty voiding?
reasoning_map.why: Visible blood needs evaluation even when painless and intermittent.
reasoning_map.if_present: Clots, retention or significant bleeding require urgent assessment.
reasoning_map.if_absent: Without these complications, arrange prompt investigation rather than dismissing resolved bleeding.
reasoning_map.next_action: Review smoking, exposures and medications; track a urology referral.
reasoning_map.document: Record the answer and findings only if obtained; keep possible diagnoses in Assessment and proposed investigations in Plan.

content_revisions.round2: Atomic history disclosures; onset versus episode duration; coherent position/comfort responses; authored voiding clarification. Natural-question router validation remains separate.
content_revisions.round3: Question dimensions restricted to authored temporal content; complete medication sentences retain original scope, doses and timing; causal assessment aliases require the stated etiology. No new case findings; author-reviewed, not clinician approved.
content_revisions.round4: Exact opening and per-speech-version disclosure contracts; removed borrowed opening atoms; split previously unspoken negative-history qualifiers; explicit current status and last-known-well routes. Existing clinical facts and IDs preserved; no clinician approval.
